Reductive amination is a chemical reaction that involves the conversion of an aldehyde or ketone to an amine through the reduction of the carbonyl group. This process typically requires a reducing agent, such as sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) or hydrogen gas (H₂) in the presence of a metal catalyst like palladium on carbon (Pd/C).

The general reaction can be described as follows:

\[ \text{R-CO-X} + \text{R'-NH}_2 + \text{Reductant} \rightarrow \text{R-CH(NH}_2\text{)-R'} + \text{X}^{-} \]

Where:
- R and R' are alkyl or aryl groups.
- X is a leaving group (e.g., -OH, -OR, -Cl, etc.) in the case of aldehydes, or -OR' in the case of ketones.
- The reductant is used to reduce the carbonyl group (C=O) to a primary amine (-CH(NH₂)-).

This reaction is widely used in organic synthesis to form amine functionalities, which are important in the synthesis of drugs, natural products, and other organic compounds.
